1999 (MCMXCIX) was a common year starting on Friday in the Gregorian calendar. It was the 19999th year of the Common Era (CE) and Anno Domini (AD) designations, the 999th year of the 2nd millennium, the 99th year of the 20th century, and the 10th and last year of the 1990s decade. Also, it was designated by the United Nations as the International Year of Older Persons. January 1 – The euro is established. January 2 – A snowstorm leaves 14 inches (359 mm) of snow in Milwaukee, Wisconsin and 21 inches (533.4 mm) in Chicago, Illinois, killing 68. January 4 – Gunmen open fire on Shia Muslims worshiping in a mosque in Islamabad, Pakistan, killing 16 and injuring 25. January 6 – Dennis Hastert becomes Speaker of the United States House of Representatives. January 8 – 3.4 million copies of the movie The Rescuers is recalled after a photo of a topless woman was discovered in two of the 110,000 slides in that scene of the movie. January 10 – A large piece of the chalk cliff at Beachy Head collapses into the sea. January 11 – Bülent Ecevit, of DSP forms the new government of Turkey (56th government, an interim government ) January 20 – The China News Service announces new government restrictions on Internet use aimed especially at Internet cafes. January 21 – In one of the largest drug busts in American history, the United States Coast Guard intercepts a ship with over 9,500 pounds (4.3 tons) of cocaine aboard, headed for Houston, Texas. January 25 – A 6.1 Richter scale earthquake hits western Colombia, killing at least 1,000. February 2 – Hugo Chávez becomes President of Venezuela. February 4 – Unarmed West African immigrant Amadou Diallo is shot dead by NYC police officers on an unrelated stake-out, inflaming race relations in the city. February 7 – King Hussein of Jordan dies from cancer, and his son Abdullah II inherits the throne. February 10 – Avalanches in the French Alps near Geneva kill at least 10. February 11 – Pluto moves along its eccentric orbit further from the Sun than Neptune. It had been nearer than Neptune since 1979, and will become again in 2231. February 16 – In Uzbekistan, an apparent assassination attempt against President Islom Karimov takes place at government headquarters. February 16 – Across Europe, Kurdish rebels take over embassies and hold hostages after Turkey arrests one of their rebel leaders. February 21 – The Albertinkatu shootings in Helsinki, Finland: Three men are killed and 1 wounded at a shooting range. February 22 – Moderate Iraqi Shiite cleric Mohammad Mohammad Sadeq al-Sadr is assassinated. February 23 – Kurdish rebel leader Abdullah Öcalan is charged with treason in Ankara, Turkey. February 23 – White supremacist John William King is found guilty of kidnapping and killing African American James Byrd Jr. by dragging him behind a truck for 2 miles (3 km). February 23 – An avalanche destroys the village of Galtür, Austria, killing 31. February 24 – LaGrand Case: The State of Arizona executes Karl LaGrand, a German national involved in an armed robbery that led to a death. Karl's brother Walter is executed a week later, in spite of Germany's legal action in the International Court of Justice to attempt to save him. February 27 – While trying to circumnavigate the world in a hot air balloon, Colin Prescot and Andy Elson set a new endurance record after being aloft for 233 hours and 55 minutes. March 1 – One of 4 bombs detonated in Lusaka, Zambia, destroys the Angolan Embassy. March 1 – Rwandan Hutu rebels kill and dismember 8 foreign tourists at the Buhoma homestead, Uganda. March 1 – The Convention on the Prohibition of Anti-Personnel Mines comes into force. March 2 – The brand new Mandalay Bay hotel and casino opens in Las Vegas. March 3 – Walter LaGrand is executed in the gas chamber in Arizona. March 4 – In a military court, United States Marine Corps Captain Richard J. Ashby is acquitted of the charge of reckless flying which resulted in the deaths of 20 skiers in the Italian Alps, when his low-flying jet hit a gondola cable. March 12 – Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic join NATO. March 15 – In Brussels, Belgium, the Santer Commission resigns over allegations of corruption. March 17 – The Roth IRA is introduced by U.S. Senator William V. Roth, Jr. March 21 – Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones become the first to circumnavigate the Earth in a hot air balloon. March 21 – The 71st Academy Awards are held at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles, California with Shakespeare in Love winning Best Picture. March 23 – Gunmen assassinate Paraguay's Vice President Luis María Argaña. March 24 – NATO launches air strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which refused to sign a peace treaty. This marks the first time NATO has attacked a sovereign country. March 24 – Fire in the Mont Blanc Tunnel kills 39 people, closing the tunnel for nearly 3 years. March 25 – Enron energy traders allegedly route 2,900 megawatts of electricity destined for California to the town of Silver Peak, Nevada, population 200. March 26 – The Melissa worm attacks the Internet. March 26 – A Michigan jury finds Dr. Jack Kevorkian guilty of second-degree murder for administering a lethal injection to a terminally ill man. March 27 – Kosovo War: A U.S. F-117 Nighthawk is shot down by Serbian forces. March 29 – For the first time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closes above the 10,000 mark, at 10,006.78. April 5 – In Laramie, Wyoming, Russell Henderson pleads guilty to kidnapping and felony murder, in order to avoid a possible death penalty conviction for the apparent hate crime killing of Matthew Shepard. June 1 – Napster, a revolutionary music downloading service, debuts. June 1 - American Airlines Flight 1420 overruns the runway in Little Rock, Arkansas killing 11 people. June 2 – After decades of fighting off outside technological influences like television, the King of Bhutan allows television transmissions to commence in the Kingdom for the first time, coinciding with the King's Silver Jubilee (see Bhutan Broadcasting Service). June 5 – The Islamic Salvation Army, the armed wing of the Islamic Salvation Front, agrees in principle to disband in Algeria. June 6 – In Brazil, 345 prisoners escape from Putim prison through the front gate. June 8 – The government of Colombia announces it will include the estimated value of the country's illegal drug crops, exceeding half a billion US dollars, in its gross national product. June 9 – Kosovo War: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and NATO sign a peace treaty. June 10 – Kosovo War: NATO suspends its air strikes after Slobodan Milošević agrees to withdraw Serbian forces from Kosovo. June 12 – Kosovo War – Operation Joint Guardian/Operation Agricola begins: NATO-led United Nations peacekeeping forces KFOR enter the province of Kosovo in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. June 12 – Texas Governor George W. Bush announces he will seek the Republican Party nomination for President of the United States. June 14 – Thabo Mbeki is elected President of South Africa. June 18 – The J18 international anti-globalization protests are organized in dozens of cities around the world, some of which lead to riots. June 21 – Apple Computer releases the first iBook, a Laptop designed specifically for average consumers. June 23 – The Phillips explosion of 1999 kills 2 and injures 3 in Pasadena, Texas. 1 July – The Scottish Parliament is officially opened by Queen Elizabeth on the day that legislative powers are officially transferred from the old Scottish Office in London to the new devolved Scottish Executive in Edinburgh. Furrow, Jr. wounds 5 and kills 1 during the August 1999 Los Angeles Jewish Community Center shooting. Senior Army generals refuse to accept the dismissal. Musharraf, who is out of the country, attempts to return in a commercial airliner. Sharif orders the Karachi airport to not allow the plane to land. The generals lead a coup d'état, ousting Sharif's administration and taking over the airport. 1998 (MCMXCVIII) was a common year starting on Thursday in the Gregorian calendar. January 1 – Smoking is banned in all California bars and restaurants. January 2 - Russia begins to circulate new rubles to stem inflation and promote confidence. January 2 - A gunman shoots Antario Teodoro Filho, Brazilian politician and radio presenter, in the middle of his broadcast. January 4-10 - A massive ice storm, caused by El Nino, strikes New England, southern Ontario and Quebec, resulting in widespread power failures, severe damage to forests, and a number of deaths. January 4 – Wilaya of Relizane massacres of 4 January 1998 in Algeria; over 170 killed in three remote villages. January 6 – The Lunar Prospector spacecraft is launched into orbit around the Moon and later found evidence for frozen water on the moon's surface. January 8 - Ramzi Yousef is sentenced to life in prison for planning the World Trade Center bombing. January 8 - Cosmologists announce that the expansion rate of the universe is increasing. January 11 – Sidi-Hamed massacre in Algeria; over 100 people killed. January 12 – 19 European nations agree to forbid 1998 like a 1999 one human cloning. January 14 – Researchers in Dallas, Texas present findings about an enzyme that slows aging and cell death (apoptosis). January 15 – The stalker of Howard Stern, Lance Carvin, is sentenced to years for threatening to kill Stern and his family. January 16 – NASA announces that John Glenn will return to space when Space Shuttle Discovery blasts off in October 1998. January 17 – Paula Jones accuses President Bill Clinton of sexual harassment. January 22 – Suspected "Unabomber" Theodore Kaczynski pleads guilty and accepts a sentence of life without the possibility of parole. January 26 - Lewinsky scandal: On American television, Bill Clinton denies he had "sexual relations" with former White House intern Monica Lewinsky. January 26 - Compaq buys Digital Equipment Corporation. January 27 – American First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton appears on the Today show calling the attacks against her husband part of a "vast right-wing conspiracy." January 28 - Ford Motor Company announces the buyout of Volvo Cars for $6.45 billion. January 28 - Gunmen hold at least 400 children and teachers hostage for several hours at an elementary school in Manila, Philippines. January 29 – In Birmingham, Alabama a bomb explodes at an abortion clinic killing one and severely wounding another. Serial bomber Eric Rudolph is suspected as the culprit. February 3 - A low-flying US military airplane cuts the cable of a cable car near Trento, Italy, killing 20 people. February 3 - President of Armenia Levon Ter-Petrosian resigns. February 4 - A magnitude 6.1 earthquake kills more than 5,000 people in Northeastern Afghanistan. February 7-22 - The 1998 Winter Olympics are held in 1998 like a 2000 one for Nagano, Japan. February 16 - China Airlines Flight 676 crashes into a residential area near Chiang Kai-shek Airport in Taipei, killing 202 people, including 6 on the ground. February 20 - Saddam Hussein negotiates a deal with UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, allowing weapons inspectors to return to Baghdad, preventing military action by the US and the UK. February 20-March 27 - The 1998 Auckland power crisis lasts five weeks. February 22-23 - The 1998 Kissimmee tornado outbreak strikes central Florida, including Orlando. Forty-two people are killed. February 26 - A solar eclipse is seen over the Caribbean Sea. March 2 - Data sent from the Galileo probe indicates that Jupiter's moon Europa has a liquid ocean under a thick crust of ice. March 2 - In Austria, Natascha Kampusch is kidnapped by Wolfgang Priklopil, being held in captivity until August 2006. March 11 - Prime Minister of Denmark Poul Nyrup Rasmussen is re-elected. March 24 - A cyclone hits Bangladesh. March 26 - In Algeria, 52 people are killed in the Oued Bouaicha massacre. April 5 - The Akashi-Kaikyo Bridge is opened to traffic in Japan, connecting Honshu and Shikoku. April 6 - Pakistan tests a medium-range missile. April 10 - In Northern Ireland the Good Friday Agreement is signed by the British and Irish governments and most political parties in Northern Ireland. April 29 - The Kyoto Protocol is signed. May 11 - India conducts 3 underground nuclear tests. May 21 - Suharto resigns as President of Indonesia, with Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie succeeding him. May 26 - Bear Grylls becomes the youngest British person to climb Mount Everest. May 28 – Pakistan explodes 5 nuclear devices. May 30 - A magnitude 6.6 earthquake kills up to 5,000 people in Afghanistan. June 3 - An ICE high speed train derails at Eschede between Hanover and Hamburg, killing 101 people. June 7 - The Guinea-Bissau Civil War begins. June 30 - Joseph Estrada becomes the 13th President of the Philippines. July 5 - Japan launches a probe to Mars. July 6 - Hong Kong International Airport opens. July 12 - The France national football team wins the FIFA World Cup on home soil against the Brazil national football team, 3-0. July 17 - At a conference in Rome 120 countries vote to create an International Criminal Court. July 17 - A tsunami is triggered by an undersea earthquake off Papua New Guinea, destroying 10 villages and killing thousands of people. July 17 - 80 years after being executed Tsar Nicholas II of Russia and his family are buried at the St. Catherine chapel in Saint Petersburg. August 2 - The Second Congo War begins. August 7 - Andres Pastrana Arango becomes President of Colombia. August 7 - During major flooding the Yangtze River breaks through the main bank, with the death toll exceeding 12,000 people. August 7 - The US Embassies in Nairobi, Kenya and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania are bombed, killing 224 people. Al-Qaeda is believed to be responsible. August 10 - Jamil Mahuad becomes President of Ecuador. August 15 - The Omagh bombing is carried out by the IRA in Northern Ireland. August 17 - Bill Clinton admits having an affair with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. August 24 - The first RFID human implantation is tested in the United Kingdom. August 28 - Said Musa becomes Prime Minister of Belize. September 2 - Swissair Flight 111, travelling from New York City to Geneva, crashes off the coast of Peggys Cove, Nova Scotia, Canada, killing all 229 people on board. September 4 - Google Inc. is founded in California by Sergey Brin and Larry Page. September 27 - After 16 years as Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, Helmut Kohl of the CDU is voted out, with the SPD's Gerhard Schroeder being elected to succeed him. October 3 - John Howard is elected to a second term as Prime Minister of Australia. October 8 - Oslo Gardermoen Airport opens. October 14 - Eric Robert Rudolph is charged with four bombings in Atlanta, Georgia in 1996. October 16 - While receiving medical treatment in the UK, Augusto Pinochet is put under house arrest under an arrest warrant from Spain. October 17 - 1,082 people are killed when an oil pipeline in Nigeria explodes. October 27 - Gerhard Schroeder becomes Chancellor of Germany, officially succeeding Helmut Kohl. October 29 - Hurricane Mitch makes landfall in Central America, causing a large amount of destruction and killing over 18,000 people across Honduras, Nicaragua and El Salvador. November 3 - Hurricane Mitch weakens after leaving a trail of destruction across Central America. November 20 - A Russian Proton rocket is launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. November 26 - Tony Blair becomes the first Prime Minister of the United Kingdom to speak at the Irish Parliament. December 6 - Hugo Chávez is elected President of Venezuela, taking office in February 1999. December 16 - Bill Clinton orders air strikes on Iraq. December 29 - Khmer Rouge leaders apologise for the genocide committed in Cambodia under Pol Pot's rule. December 31 - An extra leap second is added onto the end of the year. The UK general election, 1997 was an election held on 1 May 1997 to elect 659 members to the House of Commons of the United Kingdom. The three main candidates to become Prime Minister are shown to the right: The Labour Party and its leader Tony Blair gained the majority of seats and created the first Labour government since 1979. The Labour Party won 418 seats which was the highest majority of seats for any party since the Conservatives in the 1931 General Election. The Conservative Party suffered it's lowest number of seats since 1906 and lost all of its seats in Scotland and Wales. Several prominent Conservative politicians lost their seats such as Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth as well as Edwina Currie, David Mellor and Ian Lang. The Liberal Democrats won 46 seats, which was the highest number of seats for a third party since 1929. The Referendum Party ran on the single issue of taking Britain out of the European Union and won 2.6% of the vote but no seats. The 19th century lasted from 1801 to 1900. Some people call this the Victorian era because Queen Victoria ruled the United Kingdom. The Second Industrial Revolution started in most western countries during this century. 1830: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints is established on 6 April. 1844: Persian Prophet the Báb founds Bábism. The 19th G7 summit was a meeting in 1993 for the leaders of Canada, the European Commission, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States. The international group of leaders were together in Japan from July 7-9, 1993. The meetings were held at the State Guesthouse (Akasaka Palace) in Tokyo. The Tokyo summit of the Group of Seven (G7) was the 19th meeting in a series which began in 1976. Two previous G7 summit was hosted by Japan at Tokyo (1979 and 1986). The G8 and the summit are part of a consultation process. The G8 is not an international organization. It is an informal group. The participants were the "core members" of the group: This was the first international summit for Prime Minister Campbell and for President Clinton. The G7 leaders agreed to work on common strategies for global economic growth; and they discussed Strengthening efforts related to nuclear nonproliferation The group of leaders called for an "international agreement" to "protect forests." There is little evidence of follow-up.

19th-century French literature means the novels, poems, plays, essays, and other works written in French between 1800 and 1900. It is one of the best-known parts of French literature. Many works from this period are still read and made into films today. The century began soon after the French Revolution of 1789. It ended after the Third Republic had become firmly established. During these hundred years, France changed its form of government about seven times. Each change affected the way people wrote, printed, and read books. Several major literary movements developed during the century. Romanticism came first. It placed strong feelings, personal memories, and freedom at the centre of writing. Realism followed. It described the modern world, ordinary lives, and social relations without trying to make them more beautiful than they were. Naturalism added ideas taken from science. Symbolism looked for meanings hidden behind the visible world. These movements did not simply replace one another. They existed at the same time, borrowed ideas from each other, and often disagreed. Balzac can be seen as both a romantic and a realist. Flaubert kept many ideas from Romanticism. Naturalism, decadence, and Symbolism all existed together during the 1880s. This article deals mainly with works written in France. Literature in French was also produced in Belgium, Switzerland, Quebec, Haiti, Louisiana, Mauritius, and Réunion during the same century. These literatures have their own histories. Only the traditions most closely connected with literary life in France are discussed here. The novel became the most popular form of literature. Balzac, Stendhal, Sand, Flaubert, Zola, and Maupassant wrote novels that are read around the world. Poetry changed even more. Baudelaire, Verlaine, Rimbaud, and Mallarmé broke many of the old rules of poetry. Later poets in Europe and America followed their example. The theatre reached a larger public than most printed works. It moved from popular and noisy melodrama to the public arguments caused by romantic drama, and then to small experimental theatres at the end of the century. Writing also became a business. Cheap newspapers, low-cost books, and better schools created a much larger reading public. Some writers became rich. Others complained that art had become only another product to be sold. France changed its government many times during the century. This was important for literature because each government had its own rules about what people could print. Napoleon ruled from 1799 to 1815, first as consul and then as emperor. His government was strong, and the police watched writers closely. After his fall came the Bourbon Restoration (1815–1830). The brothers of the executed king returned to the throne. Louis XVIII ruled first, followed by Charles X. The July Revolution of 1830 removed Charles X after three days of fighting. Louis Philippe I became "King of the French". This period is called the July Monarchy (1830–1848). It was a time when the middle class became more powerful. A revolution in February 1848 created the Second Republic. It lasted only a short time. In December 1851, Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte took power by force. A year later, he became Emperor Napoléon III. His Second Empire lasted until 1870. France lost the Franco-Prussian War in 1870, and the Empire fell. In the spring of 1871, the city of Paris rose against the new government and set up its own government, the Paris Commune. The army of the new republic defeated it after a week of street fighting in May. The Third Republic followed. It was not secure at first, but it lasted until 1940. In the 1880s, it passed laws that helped shape modern France. These included the press law of 29 July 1881 and the school laws of Jules Ferry in 1882. In 1800, France was still mostly a country of farms and villages. By 1900, it had railways, factories, department stores and large cities. Paris grew very quickly. Between 1853 and 1870, much of the city was rebuilt with wide, straight streets. Old and crowded districts were pulled down. Writers described this new city with both wonder and anger. The railways also changed reading habits. Travellers needed something to read on the train. In 1853, the publisher Hachette opened bookshops in railway stations and started a cheap series of books for railway journeys. Science became very important and respected. People saw doctors, chemists and biologists as models of clear thinking. Many novelists tried to use scientific methods in their own work. Religion remained important, but people argued about it. Some writers returned to the Catholic Church. Others attacked the Church and instead believed in progress, in the people, or in art itself. Historians divide the century in different ways. No single division explains everything. One common plan uses four periods. From 1800 to 1830, old and new styles lived side by side. From 1830 to 1848, romanticism was at its strongest. From 1848 to 1870, realism grew, and poets gave more attention to form. From 1870 to 1900, naturalism and symbolism were both important. Another plan follows the political changes listed above. A third looks at changes in the way books were made and sold. One scholar has pointed out that any choice of dates can seem both natural and unfair. A century that runs from Chateaubriand's René to Jarry's Ubu roi makes sense, but a period running from 1795 to 1912 could also make sense. The story of 19th-century French writing is also the story of a new reading public. Between 1800 and 1900, the number of French people who could read grew greatly, and books became much cheaper. At the start of the century, most French people could not read well. Schooling was not free and was not required. The July Monarchy made the first large effort to change this. A law of 28 June 1833, named after the minister François Guizot, told every commune to open a public primary school and pay a teacher. In 1834 alone, about 2,275 new schools opened. There were also 15 new teacher-training colleges, added to the 47 that already existed. The results can be measured. Among young men called up for the army, the share who could not read fell from about 60 per cent in 1830 to about 40 per cent in 1860. The next step came under the Third Republic. The Jules Ferry laws of 1881 and 1882 made primary schooling free, required and non-religious. This slow growth in literacy did not change literature at once. In the first half of the century, most readers of serious books still came from the middle and upper classes. Books were expensive around 1820. A new novel cost more than a worker earned in several days. Many readers therefore used a cabinet de lecture, a reading room where people could read or borrow books for a small payment. Cheap printed books were also sold from door to door by travelling sellers. Cafés were important too. A café bought newspapers, and any customer could read them. Cafés and reading rooms helped people with small incomes to read newspapers and books. The year 1836 changed French publishing. Until then, a year's subscription to a Paris newspaper cost about 80 francs. Only a few thousand people paid for a subscription. In that year, Émile de Girardin started a newspaper called La Presse. He sold advertising space and used the money to cut the price of a subscription in half, from 80 to 40 francs. His rival Dutacq did the same with a newspaper called Le Siècle. More readers meant more power. Newspapers became places for political arguments and literary quarrels. They also helped to create what people began to call public opinion. The press also grew in variety. There were government papers, royalist papers, Catholic papers, papers for women, papers for children, and papers for farmers or doctors. Cheap papers for learning also appeared. Le Magasin pittoresque, started in 1833, published a weekly illustrated encyclopedia for families. Its subscription was very cheap, and its articles were written in plain language. To keep readers buying the newspaper every day, editors printed novels in small parts. This form is called the roman-feuilleton, or serial novel. The first serial novel printed in the French press was La Vieille fille by Balzac, in 1836. It caused a scandal because it described the frustrations of an unmarried woman very directly. The form soon became very successful. Les Mystères de Paris by Eugène Sue, published from 1842 to 1843, described crime and poverty in the dark streets of the capital. Readers from every social class followed it. Les Trois Mousquetaires and Le Comte de Monte-Cristo by Alexandre Dumas were also published as serials in 1844. Serial writing shaped the novels themselves. Each part had to end at an exciting moment. Characters had to be easy to remember over many months. Some writers thought this was harmful. Others used the pressure to write faster and better. Books slowly became cheaper. In 1838, the publisher Gervais Charpentier began a small-format series that greatly lowered prices. By the 1850s, a novel could cost 1 franc from Charpentier and 2 francs from Calmann-Lévy. At that time, the average daily pay of a Paris worker was 3.81 francs in 1853 and 4.98 francs in 1871. In 1853, Hachette opened bookshops in railway stations and printed a cheap series for travellers. Pictures also became cheaper to print, thanks to woodcut and lithography. Books with pictures reached people who might not have bought books without them. Writing for children became a separate part of publishing during the century. It began with magazines. Middle-class families wanted books and magazines that taught their moral values, and publishers produced them. The subjects included history, religion, society and, above all, science, with a strong belief in progress. Literature itself took up surprisingly little space. Some well-known authors also wrote for children. Delphine de Girardin published tales for young readers in 1832, and Marceline Desbordes-Valmore published a book for mothers and children in 1840. The most widely read children's author of the Second Empire was the Comtesse de Ségur. She published about twenty books between 1857 and 1869. Her stories end happily, but before the happy ending they show illness, poverty and cruelty quite directly. Jules Verne's books were published for young readers. For a long time, this kept his work off the shelves of serious literature. Writers were never completely free during the century. Under Napoleon and the Restoration, newspapers needed permission to publish. They also had to place large sums of money with the state as a guarantee for good behaviour. Theatres needed a licence, and censors read plays before they could be performed. The press was freer between 1830 and 1835, but the government then controlled it again. Censorship continued under the Second Empire. The year 1857 shows this clearly. Flaubert and Baudelaire were both taken to court within six months of each other. The same public prosecutor accused both writers of offending public morals and religion. Flaubert was found not guilty. Baudelaire was fined, and six poems were ordered to be removed from his book. The press law of 29 July 1881 finally gave French newspapers wide freedom. The money that writers earned shows how large the literary market had become. Under the Second Empire, a junior civil servant in Paris earned about 2,000 francs a year, and a professor at the Sorbonne earned about 12,000. The Comtesse de Ségur, whose books sold in large numbers, could receive about 3,000 francs for one book. Serious literature paid much less at first. Flaubert was paid 800 francs for a print run of 6,750 copies of Madame Bovary. The trial made the book famous, and about 30,000 copies were sold in the five years after publication. Later in the century, the best-selling novelists earned a great deal. Zola made enough money from his novels to buy a country house at Médan. Between these two groups were the many writers who lived by journalism. For many authors, reviewing plays, writing columns and producing serial novels were ways to earn a living. Writers also began to organise. The Société des gens de lettres held its first general meeting on 16 April 1838 to protect writers' income and rights. Abel-François Villemain was its first president. Balzac was elected president in 1839, and Victor Hugo joined its committee in the same year. Not everybody was happy about the new market. In an article of 1839, the critic Sainte-Beuve used the phrase "industrial literature" to attack writing made to order for a known audience. He also complained that newspapers had become dependent on advertising. The same complaint returned throughout the century. People continued to argue about whether the state should support literature or the market should decide its future. The debate was still open in 1900. The Académie française, founded in 1635, remained the most respected literary body. Election to it was a public honour. Hugo entered in 1841. Many other important writers, among them Balzac, Flaubert, Baudelaire and Zola, were never elected. Most French literary life was centred in Paris. Publishers, theatres, newspapers, critics and wealthy readers were all there. Two sides of Paris appear again and again in the books of the period. On the left bank were students, cheap rooms and places to work. On the right bank, from the Palais-Royal to the boulevards, were theatres, bookshops, fashionable cafés, gambling and entertainment. Between these two worlds, a new way of life grew after 1830: bohemia. It included artists and young people from the middle class who had left their families, some for a few years and others for good. The contrast between Paris and the provinces became one of the strongest themes in the French novel. A young man arrives from the country, is amazed by the capital, tries to rise in society and is usually defeated. Balzac used this pattern in Illusions perdues. Flaubert reversed it in Madame Bovary, where the dream of Paris remains only a dream. Zola's family series begins in a southern town and later moves beyond it. Two different images of the artist appeared during these years. Both were partly ways of presenting oneself to society. The dandy dressed with great care, said little and treated life as a work of art. The model came from England. Gautier, with his famous red waistcoat, and later Baudelaire and Barbey d'Aurevilly, all took on this role. The bohemian was the opposite: poor, untidy and often proud of this way of life. In 1830, a group of young writers formed the Petit Cénacle, named after Hugo's group. They defended pure art and enjoyed shocking other people. Nerval and Gautier belonged to it. Both figures were answers to the same problem. Writers no longer depended on noble patrons, but they did not want to think of themselves as ordinary tradesmen either. Becoming a dandy or a bohemian was one way of rejecting both roles. By the 1880s, this world had moved to Montmartre, with its cabarets and small magazines. The famous cabaret Le Chat noir opened there in 1881. Romanticism was the first important literary movement of the century in France. It came later than in Germany or Britain, and people argued about it for about thirty years. Romanticism had several important ideas. Writers wanted freedom from the rules of 17th-century classical art. They gave a central place to feeling, memory and the self. They were interested in the Middle Ages, faraway countries, dreams and death. Many of them also believed that writers had a public duty. The writers born just before the Revolution grew up in a world that had changed greatly. Their books are full of young men who cannot find a place in society. Chateaubriand (1768–1848) is the best-known writer of this generation. His long essay Génie du christianisme appeared in 1802, the same year Victor Hugo was born. It defended the Christian religion by arguing that it was beautiful and had inspired great art. Two short stories connected with that book, Atala (1801) and René (1802), made him famous in another way. René is a young man who feels empty and bored but cannot explain why. This sadness without a clear cause was later called le mal du siècle, the sickness of the age. Chateaubriand's own memoirs, Mémoires d'outre-tombe, were published after his death. Madame de Staël (1766–1817) argued that literature depends on the society that produces it. Her book De l'Allemagne was printed in London in 1813 and in Paris in May 1814. In it, she praised German writers and defended imagination against imitation. Because she had opposed Napoleon, people read her book as a political act as well as a literary one. Benjamin Constant wrote Adolphe (1816), a short novel written in a cold and controlled style about a love affair that neither person can end. Senancour wrote Obermann (1804), a book of letters from a man who withdraws from the world. The argument between the old school and the new first took place in magazines before it reached the theatre. The young Hugo started Le Conservateur littéraire in 1819. It was royalist, and it lasted until 1821. In 1823, Hugo joined Émile Deschamps and others to start La Muse française, which supported a more confident form of romanticism. A liberal newspaper, Le Globe, was started in 1824. It gave space to the new writing and helped to move romanticism away from royalism and towards liberal politics. The two sides used strong words. Supporters of classical writing said that the new poetry was barbarous and unreasonable. The romantics answered by defending feeling and inspiration. La Muse française closed in 1824 after one of its own contributors changed sides in an attempt to win a seat at the Académie française. Private meetings were as important as printed reviews. Charles Nodier became librarian at the Arsenal and held evenings there. They brought together older and younger writers and supporters of both classical and romantic writing. Hugo's own group met later in the 1820s. Under the July Monarchy, large literary reviews became more important. The Revue des Deux Mondes published criticism, foreign literature and new fiction, and became the most respected of them. French romanticism drew more strongly on literature from other countries than any earlier French literary movement. England gave French writers two important models. Walter Scott showed them how to write the historical novel. Lord Byron provided a different model: proud, unhappy, mocking and in revolt. His complete works began to appear in France in 1818. His death in 1824 while helping the Greeks made this image even stronger. A story about a vampire, said at the time to be by Byron, was translated in 1819. It helped to make vampire stories popular in France, and this interest later reached Baudelaire. German literature offered another model: the dreaming and suffering young man, represented by Goethe's Werther. German writing also encouraged religious and philosophical thought. August Wilhelm Schlegel's lectures on drama were translated in December 1813 and directly attacked the French dramatic system. William Shakespeare became an important model for the romantics. English companies performed Shakespeare in Paris in the 1820s, and they had a strong effect on young writers. The translation and performance of Othello in 1829 was itself a political act. The influence of foreign literature continued later in the century. Edgar Allan Poe became known in France through Baudelaire's translations. Charles Dickens and the English novel were widely read. Russian writers, above all Tolstoy, became important in the 1880s. Ibsen and Strindberg reached the experimental stage soon afterwards. Much poetry at the start of the century still followed traditional forms inherited from the 18th century. A change came in March 1820, when Alphonse de Lamartine published Méditations poétiques. The book was short, but it sold very well. Lamartine wrote about love, loss, nature and God in a soft, flowing style. Nine editions appeared in two and a half years. A second collection, Nouvelles Méditations poétiques, followed in September 1823. Other poets soon followed. Alfred de Vigny published Poèmes antiques et modernes in 1826. Vigny wrote about lonely and silent strength. His poems often use a story from the Bible or from history to make a point about human life. Marceline Desbordes-Valmore (1786–1859) is now seen as one of the strongest voices of the group. She wrote about separation, motherhood and unhappy love. She also used unusual line lengths without making them sound forced. Victor Hugo published Odes et Ballades (1822 and after) and then Les Orientales (1829), a colourful collection of poems about Greece, Spain and the East. Alfred de Musset made fun of everyone, including the romantics themselves, in Contes d'Espagne et d'Italie (1830). Two other important romantic poets were Vigny and Musset. Alfred de Vigny (1797–1863) served for years as an army officer during peacetime. He found this life empty and later wrote from the point of view of an outsider. He gave some of his first poems to Le Conservateur littéraire and La Muse française. His historical novel Cinq-Mars (1826) was a success, and his version of Othello was performed in 1829. Vigny thought that the world is silent and that people should face it with quiet courage. Servitude et grandeur militaires (1835) is a book of three stories about soldiers who obey orders that they know are wrong. His late poems were collected after his death as Les Destinées (1864). His play Chatterton (1835) presents the poet as someone who cannot live from his work. Alfred de Musset (1810–1857) began publishing at a very young age. His first book appeared when he was twenty. It already made fun of romantic fashions while also using them. His love affair with George Sand in 1833 and 1834 ended badly and inspired works by both writers. Musset's four long poems called Les Nuits (1835–1837) present suffering as the price of poetry. La Confession d'un enfant du siècle (1836) tries to explain a whole generation through the story of one young man. Musset also wrote plays. He published them to be read rather than performed, under the title Un spectacle dans un fauteuil. Lorenzaccio (1834) is set in Florence and shows a man who becomes what he pretends to be. These plays were performed much later and are now often seen on stage. Musset drank heavily and wrote little after the age of forty. He died at forty-six. The main public argument between the old and new schools took place in the theatre. Classical French tragedy followed strict rules. A play should have one main action, take place in one location and cover no more than one day. Comic and serious scenes should not be mixed. Three texts attacked these rules. In 1823, Stendhal published a pamphlet called Racine et Shakespeare. He argued that modern audiences wanted plays about their own time. Mérimée presented his Théâtre de Clara Gazul (1825) as a translation from Spanish. Then, in December 1827, Hugo printed his play Cromwell with a long preface that set out the ideas of the new movement. Hugo's preface argued that modern art should show life as a whole, including its ugly parts. It also argued that mixing the grand and the low was true to human nature. Hugo rejected the rules of time and place, but not the rule of a single main action. He also continued to defend drama written in verse. The first major public test came on 25 February 1830. Hugo's play Hernani opened at the Comédie-Française. Hugo's young supporters filled the seats. Most of the forty-five performances were noisy. Later writers turned the evening into a legend. In fact, other first nights had been just as stormy. What made this performance important was where it happened. The argument concerned the official national stage, which both sides wanted to control. The July Revolution followed five months later, and people later connected the two events in their memories. Romantic drama was successful for about ten years. Hugo wrote Marion de Lorme and Lucrèce Borgia. Ruy Blas (1838) is often considered his best play. Alexandre Dumas wrote Antony (1831). Vigny wrote Chatterton (1835), about a poet who kills himself because society has no use for him. The failure of Hugo's Les Burgraves in 1843 is usually treated as the end of romantic drama as a major movement on stage. In the same year, Hugo's daughter Léopoldine drowned, and he stopped publishing for several years. Romanticism was not only a style. It also offered an idea of what a writer should be. The writer was often seen as a guide. Hugo said that the poet should walk in front of the people, holding a light. Vigny gave the opposite picture: the poet is misunderstood and alone. Both ideas became popular. Groups of writers met in private houses. These groups were called a cénacle. Hugo's group in the late 1820s brought together young poets, students and painters. Its energy helped to make Hernani a success. The romantic writer was also often pictured as a young man who wanted to act quickly. Writers from other countries provided important models: Lord Byron for the proud rebel, Goethe for the dreaming youth, and Walter Scott for history. Scott was very successful in France. His novel Quentin Durward (1823) was his greatest success there, partly because it is set in France and tells a story about the making of the country. Vigny's Cinq-Mars (1826) and Mérimée's Chronique du règne de Charles IX (1829) follow his example. Gérard de Nerval (1808–1855) was different from many other romantic writers. He translated Goethe's Faust when he was very young. He also travelled in Germany and the East. Nerval suffered from mental illness and was treated in hospital several times. He turned these experiences into literature. Sylvie (1853) mixes memory and dream so closely that the reader cannot easily separate them. Aurélia (1855) describes the experience of madness from within. His fourteen sonnets called Les Chimères are dense and strange, and later poets studied them closely. Nerval was found hanged in a Paris street in January 1855. His poetic way of writing prose pointed towards the prose poem. In his own time, Nerval was known as a translator, a traveller and a charming but unlucky man. Readers in the 20th century saw him differently: as an early explorer of dream, memory and the divided self. The surrealists later saw him as an important writer who had come before their own movement. They saw Lautréamont and Rimbaud in a similar way. The novel and poetry were only part of 19th-century literature. Several other kinds of writing were also important. France produced many short stories. Newspapers helped this form to grow because they needed short pieces to publish every week. The words used for the form are important. The French word conte comes from the verb meaning "to tell". A short story often makes the presence of a storyteller clear, while history usually tries to hide the person telling the story. Balzac's Le Colonel Chabert (1832) shows what the form could do. A soldier believed to have died at the battle of Eylau returns to Paris. His wife has inherited his property and married again, and nobody wants him to be alive. He ends up in an asylum, where he answers only to a number. The story places his own account against the official one, and the more powerful side wins. Charles Nodier wrote fantastic tales. Prosper Mérimée wrote short stories in a dry and exact style, including Mateo Falcone (1829), La Vénus d'Ille (1837) and Carmen (1845). Bizet later turned Carmen into the opera Carmen. Later in the century, Maupassant became one of the most important writers of short stories. Alphonse Daudet also used the form in Lettres de mon moulin (1869), as did Villiers de l'Isle-Adam. Alongside realist stories, there was also a strong tradition of tales about the supernatural and the strange. In French, this kind of writing is called the fantastique. It became popular in France in the 1830s, after Loève-Veimars translated the stories of the German writer E. T. A. Hoffmann. It also had older roots in works such as Cazotte's Le Diable amoureux (1772), Beckford's Vathek (1787) and Potocki's Manuscrit trouvé à Saragosse (1805). The last two were written in French by foreign authors, which shows how widely French was used at the time. The fantastique is not the same as the gothic novel. Instead of simply showing frightening events, it makes the reader doubt what is real. It is also often ironic, and the reader may remain unsure whether the storyteller can be believed. Charles Nodier wrote this kind of tale early in the century. La Fée aux miettes (1832) tells the story of a carpenter who marries an old beggar woman. She says that she is the Queen of Sheba and appears beautiful in his dreams. He is shut in an asylum in Glasgow, escapes, and carries a singing flower. Théophile Gautier wrote stories about dead women who return, as well as stories about drugs and dreams. Prosper Mérimée used the form in La Vénus d'Ille (1837), in which a bronze statue may or may not kill a bridegroom. Mérimée tells the story in a calm and controlled way, which makes the uncertainty stronger. Later in the century, the fantastique became connected with science. Villiers wrote about machines and artificial people. Maupassant wrote about fear, obsession and the loss of reason. The 19th century was also an important period for writing about one's own life. The Revolution had moved many people from one kind of life to another, and private memories became a subject of public interest. The Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène, published in 1823, was widely read and helped to create the Napoleonic legend. Emmanuel de Las Cases wrote it from his conversations with Napoleon on Saint Helena, so it is not simply a book written by Napoleon himself. Chateaubriand worked for many years on Mémoires d'outre-tombe, which he arranged to have published only after his death. George Sand wrote Histoire de ma vie. Stendhal left unfinished books about his own life, which were published much later. Diaries and letters were also important. The journal of the Goncourt brothers describes Paris literary life over forty years. Flaubert's letters are also read as important works in their own right. Travel books sold well and were treated as literature. Chateaubriand travelled to America and the eastern Mediterranean. Lamartine, Nerval, Gautier and Flaubert all published accounts of journeys to Egypt, Turkey or the Holy Land. Gautier also wrote about Spain and Russia. These books mix description, history, personal feeling and, quite often, invention. Modern readers can also see how much they depend on ideas about the East and about race that were common at the time but are no longer accepted. Much literary writing first appeared in newspapers and reviews. Almost every writer named in this article worked for newspapers. Gautier reviewed plays for La Presse from 1838 to 1855. Zola began his career writing publicity for books and working as a reviewer. Vallès, Barrès and Mirbeau were journalists as well as novelists. The daily column, the theatre review, the art review and the printed interview all developed into their modern forms during these years. The novel was not highly respected in 1800. Serious critics treated it as light reading and often as reading for women. By 1900, it had become the leading literary form in France. Several things caused this change. Novels could be printed in newspapers, so they reached many readers. They could describe a whole society in one book. They could also bring together history, science, politics and private life. Before Stendhal and Balzac, the French novel was widely read but not highly respected. Several kinds of novel were popular at the same time. The sentimental novel told stories of love and suffering, often through letters. People often thought of it as reading for women, and it kept some features of the 18th-century novel. The gothic novel came from Britain at the end of the 18th century. It often included ruined castles, ghosts, monks and hidden crimes. Charles Nodier gave the French form a wider name, the "frenetic" novel. This kind of writing was popular under Napoleon and the Restoration and lasted until about 1840, when the serial novel took over many of its features. Cheap novels were often badly printed and sold by travelling sellers or lent in reading rooms. The most widely read authors under Napoleon were Pigault-Lebrun and Ducray-Duminil, who are now largely forgotten. Then came the historical novel, following the example of Walter Scott. By 1830, it was the leading kind of novel. Vigny, Mérimée, Hugo and Balzac all wrote historical novels. Hugo's early Bug-Jargal (1826), set during a slave revolt in Haiti, shows how several forms could be mixed together: gothic horror, melodrama and history. Stendhal (1783–1842) was born Henri Beyle in Grenoble. He served in Napoleon's armies, lived for years in Italy, and worked as a French consul. He was almost unknown as a novelist during his lifetime. He said that he expected to be read around 1880, and he was roughly right. Le Rouge et le Noir (1830) follows Julien Sorel, a carpenter's son who is clever, proud and poor. Julien sees that under the restored monarchy, a young man of his class can rise only through the Church or by pretending to be something he is not. The novel studies ambition and self-deception. La Chartreuse de Parme (1839) is set in a small Italian court after the fall of Napoleon. Its opening pages describe the battle of Waterloo through the eyes of a young man who does not understand what he is seeing. Stendhal's style is dry and fast. He avoids decorative writing. He is especially good at showing small changes of feeling between two people who are unsure of each other. His writings about his own life, including Vie de Henry Brulard and other unfinished books, were published long after his death. Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) wrote about ninety novels and stories, as well as plays and articles. He worked at night, drank large amounts of coffee, and was always in debt. He began by writing cheap fiction under false names for reading rooms. His first success under his own name came in 1829 with Les Chouans, a historical novel, and a book about marriage. In 1835, in Le Père Goriot, he found the method that holds much of his work together. Characters return from one novel to another. A minor character in one book can become the main character of the next. Readers meet the same people at different ages. Balzac then went back and changed earlier novels so that they fitted this new plan. In 1841, he signed a contract for a complete edition of his work. Seventeen volumes appeared between 1842 and 1847 under one title, La Comédie humaine. The preface of 1842 explains the idea. Balzac compares human society with the animal world. Just as there are different species of animals, he says, there are different social types: the country doctor, the money lender, the clerk and the fashionable woman. The novelist should describe them as a naturalist describes birds. Money is everywhere in his work, and so is Paris. Illusions perdues (1837–1843) shows a young poet from the provinces destroyed by the Paris press. Eugénie Grandet (1833) shows a miser in a small town. La Peau de chagrin (1831) mixes realism with a magical object. Balzac did not believe in progress. He wrote as a monarchist and a Catholic. However, his novels show the old social order falling apart, even though this was not what he intended. Victor Hugo wrote novels over a period of sixty years, and two of them are among the best-known books in the world. Notre-Dame de Paris (1831) is set in Paris in 1482. It made readers care about medieval buildings at a time when many were being pulled down, and it helped to begin the movement to protect them. Les Misérables (1862) follows Jean Valjean, a man who was imprisoned for stealing bread. The main action takes place between 1815 and the Paris rising of 1832. Around him, Hugo presents poor people in Paris, a police inspector, a dying mother, a street child and the failed rising of 1832. The book argues openly for social reform. Les Travailleurs de la mer (1866) is set in the Channel Islands, where Hugo was living. Quatrevingt-treize (1874) returns to the Revolution. Hugo's novels do not follow the usual rules of a tightly organised plot. He often stops the story for long discussions of convents, street slang or the Paris sewers. He wanted a novel to contain many different parts of life. George Sand (1804–1876) was born Aurore Dupin. She left her husband, moved to Paris, wore men's clothes in public and used a man's pen name. She was one of the most widely read French writers of her time. Her first novels, Indiana (1832) and Lélia (1833), deal with unhappy marriage and a woman's right to choose her own life. They made her famous, but they also brought strong attacks. Sand was also a republican and a socialist, and people widely discussed her private life. Together, these things made her a model who worried many people. In 1839, she moved back to her family home at Nohant, in the Berry. She had known local farmers since childhood, and she began to write about them. Mauprat (1837) already mixes ideas with local colour. Then came La Mare au diable (1846), François le Champi (1847) and La Petite Fadette (1849). These books are short, clear and gentle. Beneath their simple style is a strong belief that ordinary people deserve respect. Sand said that she wanted people to know and like country people, and she studied them both as a scientist and as a poet would. These books also created a problem of language, and Sand knew it. She wanted to use French that a Paris reader could understand without making a country reader feel insulted. The prologue of François le Champi discusses this difficulty directly. The result is a mixed language, partly spoken and partly written, partly local and partly national. Other writers wrote about their own regions. Alphonse Daudet wrote about Provence in Lettres de mon moulin (1866–1869). Barbey d'Aurevilly wrote about Normandy. Erckmann and Chatrian wrote together about Alsace and Lorraine. Fromentin wrote about the Atlantic coast and about Algeria. Zola treated country life very differently. La Terre (1887) shows peasants fighting over land and does not try to make them likeable. This book caused a split among writers who had supported him. Interest in regional writing grew stronger after 1900, when it became an organised movement. Alongside the writers who are now studied at school, there was a very large market for popular novels. Alexandre Dumas (1802–1870) is the best known. With a team of helpers, he produced adventure novels very quickly. Les Trois Mousquetaires and Le Comte de Monte-Cristo both began to appear in 1844. Dumas mixed real history with invented events, and his dialogue moves the story forward quickly. Eugène Sue moved from sea stories to stories about society. Les Mystères de Paris (1842–1843) describes criminals, prostitutes and very poor people. Readers wrote to Sue asking him to save his characters. The book is often said to have changed the way the French middle class thought about poverty. Jules Verne (1828–1905) began publishing with the publisher Hetzel in 1863. His Voyages extraordinaires used balloons, submarines and rockets. Vingt mille lieues sous les mers (1870) and Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours (1873) are still read. Verne is one of the founders of science fiction. Historical adventures, crime stories and sentimental serials appeared in newspapers throughout the century. Most of their authors are forgotten today, but their books helped millions of people become regular readers.

The Russian First Army was a World War I Russian field army that fought on the Eastern Front for two years. It was commanded by General Paul Rennenkampf when Russia invaded East Prussia at the outbreak of war in 1914. They were accompanied by the Second Army commanded by General Alexander Samsonov. The plan was to trap the German army in a Pincer movement between the two armies. On 17 August the First Army engaged the Germans at Stallupönen. They fought the Germans again on 20 August at Gumbinnen and defeated them. Rennenkampf thought the Germans could be finished off by Samsonov's Second Army and did not move quickly enough to help them. In late August 1914 the German and Russian second army met at Tannenberg. The Second Army was encircled and suffered complete destruction. Let by General Paul von Hindenburg the Germans turned north to attack the Russian First army at First Battle of the Masurian Lakes in September 1914. The Russians fought hard but were driven back to the Russian border. Rennenkampf kept his troops in good order as they retreated. They set up defensive lines on the Russian border. After another defeat near Silesia on November 11, Rennenkampf was dismissed. He was replaced by General Litvinov. The First Army again fought at Thorn and Lódź but there was no clear cut winner. The First army evacuated Lódź and returned to their own lines for the remainder of the winter. The First Army served on the Northwestern front for the rest of the war.

2000 (MM) was a century leap year starting on Saturday in the Gregorian calendar. It was the 2000th year of the Common Era (CE) and Anno Domini (AD) designations, and the last year of the 2nd millennium and the 20th century. 2000 was designated the International Year for the Culture of Peace and the World Mathematical Year. It was also the first year of the 2000s decade. Popular culture holds the year 2000 as the first year of the 21st century and the 3rd millennium, due to a tendency to group the years according to decimal values, as if the nonexistent year zero was counted. According to the Gregorian calendar, these distinctions fall to the year 2001, because the 1st century back then was also retroactively said to start with year 1. Since the Gregorian calendar doesn't have 0 as a year, its first millennium spanned from years 1 to 1000, and its second millennium from years 1001 to 2000. For more information, see century and millennium. The year 2000 is sometimes abbreviated as "Y2K". The "Y" stands for "year", and the "K" stands for the Latin prefix "kilo-" (meaning "thousand"). Technology and certain parts of society were forced to deal with Y2K concerns, related to issues with computers not calculating dates properly after the year 1999. However, by the end of 1999, many companies had already converted to new, or upgraded, existing software. Some even obtained Y2K certification. As a result of massive effort, relatively few problems occurred. January 1 - To most people, it was the first day of the 21st century and 3rd millennium. The year 2 (II) was a common year that started on Sunday, according to the Julian calendar. According to the Gregorian calendar, it started on a Tuesday. At the time, it was known as the Year of the Consulship of Vinicius and Varus. It was the 2nd year of the 1st century. Following the death of Lucius Caesar, Livia Drusilla convinced Augustus to allow her son Tiberius back into Rome as a private citizen. This was after six years in enforced retirement on Rhodes. Gaius Caesar meets with Phraates V, the king of Parthia on the Euphrates. Publius Alfenus Varus and Publius Vinicius become Roman Consuls. Cedeides becomes Archon of Athens. Using Roman military support, Artavasdes III, son of Ariobarzanes II, king of Media Atropatene, becomes the king of Armenia. Juba II of Mauretania joins Gaius Caesar in Armenia as a military advisor. The first census is concluded in China. The census has begun the year before. Final numbers show a population of nearly 60 million (59,594,978 people in a bit more than 12 million households). The census is one of the most accurate surveys in Chinese history. The Chinese census shows nearly one million people living in Vietnam. Deng Yu, Han Dynasty general and statesman (d. 58) Lucius Caesar, son of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa and Julia the Elder. He was also the heir to the throne in Gaul. (b. 17 BC)

The 1st century was the century that lasted from year 1 to 100. During this period Europe, North Africa and the Near East fell under increasing domination by the Roman Empire. It continued expanding under the emperor Claudius (43). The reforms introduced by Augustus during his long reign stabilized the empire. Later in the century the Julio-Claudian Dynasty, which had been founded by Augustus came to an end with the death of Nero in 68. There followed the famous Year of Four Emperors, a brief period of civil war and instability, which was finally brought to an end by Vespasian, 9th Roman emperor, and founder of the Flavian Dynasty. China continued to be dominated by the Han Dynasty, despite a 14-year interruption by the Xin dynasty under Wang Mang. Han rule was restored in 23. Wang Mang's rule represents the watershed between the Western/Former Han and the Eastern/Later Han. The capital was also moved from Chang'an to Luoyang. Western Europe: Controlled by Rome. Southern Europe: Controlled by Rome. North Africa: Controlled by Rome. West Africa: Numerous tribal governments. Central Africa: Bantu tribes, collapsing Nok civilization. East Africa: Meroe, Blemmyes, Axum Empire. Southern Africa: Bantu tribes, Khoisan. Western Asia: Rome, Parthian empires, as well as many smaller tribes. Central Asia: Sarmatian tribes. South-central Asia: Kushan empire, Western Satraps, Satavahana, Tibetans. Southeast Asia: City states, Khmer, Mon kingdoms, Funan. East Asia: Eastern Han Dynasty of China, Three Kingdoms (Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla) of Korea. Early 1st century – Augustus of Primaporta (perhaps a copy of a bronze statue of ca. 20 BC) is made. It is now kept in Musei Vaticani, Braccio Nuovo, Rome. Early 1st century – Gemma Augustea is made. It is now kept at Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna. Early 1st century – House of the Silver Wedding, Pompeii, is built. Excavated in 1893, the year of the silver wedding anniversary of Italy's King Humbert and his wife, Margherita of Savoy, who have supported archaeological fieldwork at Pompeii. Early 1st century – Inner shrine, Ise, Mie, Mie Prefecture, is built. Yayoi period. 1: Lions became extinct in Western Europe. 8–23: Wang Mang temporarily overthrew the Han dynasty of China. 9: Three Roman legions were destroyed at Teutoberg Forest by Germans under the leadership of Arminius. 14: Augustus Caesar, first emperor of Rome, dies. His nephew Tiberius is his successor. 28–75: Emperor Ming of Han, Buddhism reaches China. Humans arrive on Pentecost Island and establish the Bunlap tribe, among others. 26: According to the Bible, Jesus begins his ministry. 30: Death of Jesus on the cross. Beginning of the Christian Church. 34: Conversion of Saint Paul. 44: Death of Herod Agrippa. 41–54: Rachias, an Ambassador sent from Sri Lanka to the court of Claudius. Masoretes adds vowel pointings to the text of the Tanakh, the Hebrew Bible. Buddhist monks in Sri Lanka first write down Buddha's teachings, creating the Pali canon. The regions of present-day Afghanistan, Pakistan and North India come under the control of the Kushans, a nomadic people forced out of northwest China by the Han Dynasty. Tacitus mentions the Suiones, who will one day be called the Swedes. Kaundinya, an Indian Brahmin marries Soma and establishes the Pre-Angkor Cambodian Kingdom of Funan. The Goths settle in northern Poland, which they called Gothiscandza, and shape the Wielbark culture. c. 50: Christian Council of Jerusalem. c. 52: Arrival of Apostle Thomas to Malabar, India. Beginning of Christianity in India. Mid-1st century – Wall niche, from garden in Pompeii, is made. It is now kept at Fitzwilliam Museum, University of Cambridge, England. Mid-1st century – Detail of a wall painting in the House of M. Lucretius Fronto, Pompeii, is made. July 19, 64: Great Fire of Rome, first Roman mass Persecution of Christians, earliest significant recognition of Christians in Rome. 66–73: First Jewish-Roman War. August 70: destruction of Herod's Temple in Jerusalem by the Romans under Titus. August 79: Pompeii and Herculaneum destroyed by eruption of Mount Vesuvius. Jewish Council of Jamnia. Spread of the Roman Empire, reaches largest size under Trajan. Arena (colosseum) is constructed, origin of the name Arena. Late 1st century – Cityscape, detail of a Second Style wall painting from a bedroom in the House of Publius Fannius Synistor, Boscoreale, is made. It is now at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City. The painting "Alexander the Great confronts Darius III at the Battle of Issos", detail of mosaic floor decoration from Pompeii, Italy is made. It is a Roman copy after a Greek painting of c. 310 BC, perhaps by Philoxenos or Helen of Egypt. It is now at Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples, Italy. Late 1st century – Bedroom, from the House of Publius Fannius Synistor, Boscoreale is made. It is reconstructed with later furnishings at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City. Late 1st century – Seascape, detail of a wall painting from Villa Farnesina, Rome, is made. Late 1st century – Young Woman Writing, detail of a wall painting, from Pompeii, is made. It is now kept at Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples. Late 1st century – Mausoleum under Construction, relief from the tomb of the Haterius family, Via Labicana, Rome, is made. It is now kept at Musei Vaticani, Museo Gregoriano Profano, ex Lateranese, Rome. Late 1st century – Middle-Aged Flavian Woman is made. It is now kept at Musei Vaticani, Museo Gregoriano Profano, ex Lateranese, Rome. c. Late 1st century – early 2nd century – Buddha and Attendants, from Katra Keshavdev, Mathura, Madhya Pradesh, India, is made. Kushan period. It is now kept at Mathura Museum. 1st–2nd centuries – Tomb model of a house is made. Eastern Han dynasty. It is now kept at The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City, Missouri. Codex, the first form of the modern book, appears in the Roman Empire Year 78—the beginning of the Saka Era used by South Asian calendars. Various inventions by Hero of Alexandria, including the steam turbine (aeolipile), water organ, and various other water-powered machines. In 31, the Han Dynasty Chinese engineer and statesman Du Shi (d. 38) from Nanyang invented the first known hydraulic-powered bellows to heat the blast furnace in smelting cast iron. He used a complex mechanical device that was powered by the rushing current against a waterwheel, a practice that would continue in China. Although Philo of Byzantium described the saqiya chain pump in the early 2nd century BC, the square-pallet chain pump was innovated in China during this century, mentioned first by the philosopher Wang Chong around 80 AD. Wang Chong also accurately described the water cycle in meteorology, and argued against the mainstream 'radiating influence' theory for solar eclipses, the latter of which was accepted by many, including Zhang Heng. The Chinese astronomer Liu Xin (d. 23) documented 1080 different stars, amongst other achievements. End of 1st century – codex replaces the scroll. According to the New Testament, during the reign of Tiberius, Jesus, a Jewish religious leader from Galilee, was crucified in Jerusalem on the charge of blasphemy for claiming to be the Son of God. But "God raised him from the dead" three days later, see Resurrection of Jesus. Over the next few decades his followers, following the Great Commission, including the apostle Paul, carried his message throughout the Greek-speaking regions of Asia Minor, eventually introducing it to Rome itself. Roman rulers began to persecute the new sect almost immediately (the emperor Nero accused the Christians of starting the fires that destroyed much of Rome in 64 AD), and would continue to do so for centuries, sometimes vigorously, and other times passively. Christian tradition records that all of Christ's apostles except John the Evangelist suffered martyrdom. In the 4th century, Christianity was eventually taken up by the emperor Constantine. One of his successors Julian the Apostate renounced it for paganism and again persecuted the Church. However, by the end of the 4th century, Emperor Theodosius I proclaimed Christianity as the state religion of the Roman Empire. Note: years before or after the 1st century are in italics.

The 1st century BC started on January 1, 100 BC and ended on December 31, 1 BC. An alternative name for this century is the last century BC. The AD/BC notation does not use a year zero. Scientific notation does, however, use a minus sign, so '2 BC' is equal to 'year −1'.

20 is a year in the 1st century. It was a leap year starting on Monday of the Julian calendar. At the time, it was known as the Year of the Consulship of Marcus Valerius Messalla Barbatus and Cotta. Tiberias is built on the Sea of Galilee by Herod Antipas. Galba is a Roman praetor. Marcus Valerius Messalla Barbatus becomes a consul. First year of Dihuang era of the Chinese Xin Dynasty. Philo defines philosophy as the maidservant of theology. Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, Roman statesman and governor of Syria (b. 44 BC) Vipsania Agrippina, wife of Gaius Asinius Gallus and former wife of Tiberius (b. 36 BC)

Year 200 (CC) was a leap year starting on Tuesday of the Julian calendar. Human population reaches about 257 million. Emperor Septimius Severus visits Syria, Palestine and Arabia. Palestine, benefiting from the kind policies of Severus, sees a big economic return. The province of Numidia is taken from the African proconsul and made an Imperial province. Rudrasena I, Saka ruler of the Western Satrap dynasty, becomes king of Malwa in ancient India. Chinese warlord Cao Cao defeats Yuan Shao in the Battle of Guandu. In Japan, Himiko, whose capital is in Yamatai, extends her authority over a number of clans. Empress Jingu sends a Japanese fleet to invade Korea. The Koreans surrender at the sight of the huge multi-oared ships and offer tribute. The Classic Age of Maya civilization begins (around this year). The Paracas culture in the Andes comes to an end (around this year). Septimius Severus, Julia Domna and their children, Publius Septimius Geta and Caracalla, from Fayum, Egypt, is made. It is now kept at Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Preussischer Kulturbesitz, Antikensammlung. Jewish Eretz Yisraeli scholar Judah ha-Nasi puts together tracts of the Mishnah. This begins the making of Talmudic law. Clement of Alexandria says to not use musical instruments to support human voices in Christian music. Brahmanism changes into Hinduism (approximate date). Fei Yi, an official of Shu (approximate date) (d. 253) Marcus Claudius Tacitus, Roman Emperor (d. 276) Mi Heng, renowned scholar and friend of Kong Rong (executed by Huang Zu) (b. 173) Sun Ce, 25, elder brother of the founder of Wu Kingdom, Sun Quan (b. 175)

2001 (MMI) was a common year starting on Monday in the Gregorian calendar. It was the first year of the 3rd millennium and 21st century. The 3rd millennium and 21st century begin on this day according to the Gregorian calendar. But popular culture holds these distinctions to January 1, 2000. A nine foot tall rock was placed by an artist in Seattle's Magnuson Park, like the one in 2001: A Space Odyssey. The U.S. crew was jailed for 10 days and the Chinese pilot, Wang Wei, went missing and thought to be dead. The Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation Between the People's Republic of China and the Russian Federation (FCT) is a treaty outlining a twenty-year cooperation between China and Russia. It was signed by the leaders of the two countries, Jiang Zemin and Vladimir Putin, on July 16, 2001. The treaty describes actions that should be taken by the two countries to establish for peaceful relations and economic cooperation, as well as diplomatic and political reliance. Article 9 of the treaty has started controversy because it may be viewed as a defense pact, meaning if one of the two countries becomes involved in a war, the other country must help them. Additionally, articles A7 and A16 point at increasing military cooperation, including the sharing of "military know-how" (A16), namely, Chinese access to Russian military technology. The treaty also describes a mutual, cooperative approach to environmental technology regulations and energy conservation; and toward international finance and trade. The document affirms Russia's stand on Taiwan as "an inalienable part of China" (A5), and highlights the commitment to ensure the "national unity and territorial integrity" in the two countries (A4). Analysts have pointed out several different reasons for the FCT, mostly involving benefits for both China and Russia. China's armed forces are largely outdated, and they want to improve them. The treaty says that Russia will share their training and technology with China, which will help that. China wants a stable, consistent and affordable level of fuel shipments, especially petroleum. This goal can be better met by using Russian oil, including the construction of a Trans-Siberian oil pipeline. China wants support for its stance on Taiwan. Russia has had trouble getting capital since the dissolution of the Soviet Union. It will be able to get more capital in several ways through the treaty. They are: Russia wants to find employment for its skilled workforce. Russia wants to sell its military technology and knowledge. Russia wants to sell its large reserves of petroleum and natural gas. Both China and Russia fear the United States (especially following its strengthened geopolitical position following the September 11, 2001 attacks) becoming involved in areas which they believe should only be affected by their respective spheres of national influences and interests: for China, this largely involves Taiwan serving as a US client state, while for Russia it involves having various former Soviet Republics as US client states. Many of these do not border either country, though Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan border China, and Kazakhstan borders both. The United States, Japan and the European Union are three economic powers which have a skilled workforce and access to capital. Russia and China can more effectively compete against these powers in the world economy if Russia has access to Chinese capital and China has access to Russian training and technology.

The United Kingdom general election, 2001 was held on Thursday 7 June 2001 to elect 659 members to the British House of Commons. It was called "the quiet landslide" by the media, as the Labour Party was re-elected with another landslide result and only suffered a net loss of 5 seats, with lower turnout of 59.4%, compared to 71.3% in the previous election. Tony Blair went on to become the first Labour Prime Minister to serve a second full term in as Prime Minister.

The 2001 Massacre of Plaza de Mayo was a massacre in the Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires and its surroundings. It occurred on December 20, 2001. Five people (Carlos Almirón, Gustavo Ariel Benedetto, Diego Lamagna, Alberto Márquez and Gastón Marcelo Riva) were killed there, four others were attempted to be murdered (Marcelo Dorado, Martín Galli, Sergio Rubén Sanchéz and Paula Simonetti). Others were injured. The events occurred under the presidency of Fernando de la Rúa during the December 2001 crisis in Argentina, during which 39 people were killed, including seven children between the ages of thirteen and eighteen. The journalist Alberto Amato of the newsroom of the newspaper Clarín, a month after the massacre, referred to it with these words: “The massacre of the Plaza de Mayo... bloodied the city with a violence and unreason that recognizes as the only precedent the terrible bombardment by naval aviation in June 1955, three months before the overthrow of Juan Perón... Among other responses that the judicial investigation include those that try to know if there was a moment, and therefore an order, that the repression of the protesters was carried out with bullets. And who gave that order. Who were the civilians who shot at the protesters protected by uniformed police? Who owns the cars from which people were shot at close range and that a police chief defined with a euphemism that would be nice if it did not contain a tragedy: "civilian cars for police use..."? How was it that, if the decision of the then government was to prevent a hypothetical "takeover" of the Government House, the dead fell several blocks from the seat of power? Did some kind of “death squad” act on December 20? If Justice manages to answer these and other questions, it will elucidate another that is only tacitly formulated: what is the political will to investigate a massacre almost without precedent in the already violent contemporary history of Argentina.” Enrique Mathov, at that time Secretary of National Security: mastermind.
